| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) One replay function with a switch on the event name | A package `replay` knows every domain | Everything in one place | Identity, authorization, CI, exposure, npm and NuGet owners would edit one file; the import graph would make the replay depend on every domain |
| (b) `journal.Register(Handler{Domain, Events, Apply})` in a file of the owning domain, and `journal.ApplyUpdate` for the update rule (chosen) | A handler applies one entry in its own transaction as the owner credential and returns an outcome; `ApplyUpdate[T]` is the three-case rule of this requirement over the owner's `Narrower[T]` | The update rule exists once and is tested once; a domain adds its events without touching another's; an event type without a handler is `skipped` | A registry (frozen at start-up, R-ARCH-032) |

**Choice:** (b).

**Rationale:** The comparator is the owning page's (R-AUTHZ-031, R-EP-020, R-CI-020), and the rule that chooses between applying, skipping and suspending is this page's. Splitting them along the two owners is what the generic function does. The development agent would revisit this if a replay needs several entries at once (a handler for a batch).

**Applied:** R-HA-054 "Dispatch" and "Replay rules"; `internal/journal/replay.go`.

### Q-HA-142 · The replay reads the journal by day prefixes and reports what it cannot read

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) List the whole journal | One listing of `_journal/revocations/` | Simple | The journal is kept for as long as the operator keeps it; a restore lists years of keys for the entries of one interval |
| (b) List the UTC days from `snapshotAt - replay_margin` to now, read each object, report an object that does not decode (chosen) | `journal.DayPrefixes`; an object that is unreadable or newer than this binary reads is returned as `Unreadable` and printed `skipped`; it never stops the replay | Bounded work; one forged or damaged object cannot block the replay of the others; the output shows what was lost (H-553) | A day boundary is a prefix boundary; the margin is always rounded to whole days |

**Choice:** (b).

**Rationale:** The key layout of this requirement already names the day. The margin covers transactions that started before the snapshot and committed after it, which a day prefix includes. The development agent would revisit this if a store lists a prefix of millions of keys too slowly.

**Applied:** R-HA-054 "Replay run"; `internal/journal/object.go` (`DayPrefixes`), `internal/journal/ports.go` (`Reader`).

### Q-HA-145 · The schema check reads the restore marker after the schema state

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The marker first | A restore that commits between the two reads is missed | Simple | A replica can find the final schema step and no marker, and serve a half-restored database |
| (b) The schema state first, then the marker, in `CheckSchema` and in the report of `quader migrate status` (chosen) | The marker is committed with the step that makes the schema servable (R-BAK-021 step 2), so a state read first cannot be followed by a missing marker | No window; one extra read on the control connection every check | Two statements instead of one |

**Choice:** (b). `postgres.ErrRestoreInProgress` is a plain failure of the `schema` check (R-OPS-001), not an outage: the replica stays not ready.
**Rationale:** The order is the whole proof; a single statement would not need it but would cost every readiness check a join. Revisit if the check moves into one query.
**Applied:** R-OPS-001 `schema` check, R-ARCH-024 step 3; `internal/meta/postgres/gate.go`, `migrate.go` (`Report`).
### Q-HA-144 · How the shipper is triggered, and what `--credentials-file` holds

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

| Option | Behaviour | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| (a) A job kind that a timer on every job-running replica enqueues while the outbox holds a row; `enabled: false` deletes the rows unshipped; `--credentials-file` is a strict YAML document of the keys of `storage.s3.credentials` | One code path; bypasses the one-minute cron resolution; the audit writer stays free of Valkey | A change waits up to `ship_interval` instead of being shipped on a signal |
| (b) A signal published by the audit writer after commit | Ships at once | The audit writer gains a Valkey dependency it must not have (INV-3) |
| (c) A periodic task, and an AWS shared credentials file | Registry-only | The finest cron schedule is one minute; profiles and fallbacks are ambiguous |

**Choice:** (a). `revocation-journal-ship` is `Coalesce` in the `maintenance` queue; `internal/app/wire_journal.go` starts the timer. With `enabled: false` the same job deletes the rows without writing objects. A credentials file also switches the journal reader to listing object versions; an unknown key in it is refused, so a typo cannot fall back to the runtime credential.
**Rationale:** The interval alone meets the acceptance criterion (the object appears within `ship_interval` after the store returns). The runtime credential lacks `s3:ListBucketVersions` (R-HA-023), so a file is the way to give a restore one. Revisit when the 5 s latency matters for the recovery point, or when the restore Job's identity replaces files.
**Applied:** R-HA-054 "Outbox and shipping" is read as triggered by the interval; `internal/jobs/journal.go`, `internal/journal/ship`, `internal/app/wire_journal.go`, `internal/journal/replay/open.go`.

### Q-HA-157 · How a platform restore keeps replicas away from the restored database until the replay has run

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

| Option | Behaviour | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| (a) A marker `post_restore_in_progress` committed in the first transaction of `quader admin post-restore`, read by the schema check like `restore_in_progress`, deleted in the last transaction; the step that scales the roles lists `api`, `packages` and every pool; the replay gets a change-log notifier; the restore point is recorded so a repeat is a no-op | The restored database is not served until the replay is done, whatever the Deployments do; a pod that is already running turns not ready and learns of the replay | A failed post-restore leaves the installation not ready until it is run again |
| (b) Only scale the roles to zero and trust the operator | No code | One role forgotten, or a hook that runs after the Deployments are applied, serves the old access (audit finding H1) |
| (c) Reuse the key `restore_in_progress` | One key | `quader migrate` refuses a half-restored database by that key and names a backup that does not exist |

**Choice:** (a). The marker holds `{restoredTo, phase, startedAt}`; phase `cleaned` records that the clean-up (replica rows, pause, sessions, fix-ups, `restored_at`) committed, so a resumed run goes to the replay and does not add the revision offset or rotate the keyspace again. `post_restore_done` holds `{restoredTo, journal, at}`; a repeat for the same restore point is a no-op unless the first run skipped the journal and this one replays. A chart that keeps `postRestore.enabled` after the restore is therefore harmless to the data; it should still switch the value off, since the Job holds the owner credential.
**Rationale:** The gate has to be in the database because the Deployments cannot be trusted to be at zero when the hook runs (a post-upgrade hook runs after them). Revisit when the chart renders the Job as a pre-upgrade hook.
**Applied:** R-HA-025 steps 1 and 4; `internal/backup/postrestore`, `internal/meta/postgres/gate.go`, `cmd/quader/admin_postrestore.go`.

### Q-HA-158 · What the replay reads: every copy, from the database's own clock, and what the shipper does with a row it cannot encode

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

| Option | Behaviour | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| (a) Group the objects by ID, replay each distinct readable copy and flag the duplicates; with version listing read every version of a key and replay the ones that differ; start at the earlier of the restore point and the newest audit event of the database; quarantine an outbox row that cannot be encoded (system_state `journal_quarantined`, `quader_revocation_journal_quarantined_total`) and ship the rest | A planted copy or overwrite cannot hide the genuine entry; a wrong `--restored-to` cannot skip revocations; one bad row does not stop the journal | A forged copy is replayed as well (it can only remove or be suspended); a quarantined row's change is missing from the journal and post-restore says so |
| (b) First copy wins (as before) | Simple | The writer of a copy chooses which one is believed (audit finding H2) |
| (c) Refuse a restore that finds a duplicate | Loud | The holder of the runtime credential can block every restore |

**Choice:** (a). The alert on the counter is the chart's (`deploy/` is not edited here).
**Rationale:** Handlers are fail-closed: a removal only removes and an update is applied only when the comparator proves it narrows, so replaying more copies cannot grant. Revisit when the journal objects are signed.
**Applied:** R-HA-054 "Replay run"; `internal/journal/replay/reader.go`, `replayer.go`, `internal/blob/s3/journalstore.go` (`GetAll`), `internal/journal/ship`.

### Q-HA-163 · A red post-release check leaves the release published and is a finding, not a withdrawal

**Superseded by [Q-HA-281](#q-ha-281--tests-run-before-a-release-not-after-it) (owner, 2026-11-10): there is no post-release check.**

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The release and its artifacts stay as published; the run of `Release Docker & Helm` goes red; the finding is recorded; the fix is a commit that Semantic Release releases under the next version (chosen) | No step changes a published artifact; `gh run rerun <id> --failed` runs the check again once its cause is gone | Publication cannot be undone in the pipeline: Semantic Release has released the commits, and a re-run publishes nothing for them ([releasing.md](../developer/releasing.md#when-no-release-comes)), so a fix needs a new commit anyway | Until the fix release, the chart index lists the broken version as its newest entry, which `helm install` without `--version` takes; an image without its attestation stays under its tag |
| (b) Withdraw a red release: delete the GitHub release and the tag, remove the image tags on Docker Hub, rewrite `gh-pages` without the version | The pipeline reverts what it published | Installers no longer see the broken version | The commits have no release until a new commit lands; a deleted tag breaks anyone who pulled by tag; a rewrite of `gh-pages` is a force-push, and the job would then undo a release because of an infrastructure fault |
| (c) Run the check before the release is public (a draft release, or the check before Semantic Release) | No broken release is ever public | The strongest guarantee | The check reads the published artifacts (the chart's index on Pages, the image by its tag), so they must exist first; a draft changes the release flow that [ADR-130](../decisions.md#adr-130--the-organisations-ci-and-release-standard) fixes |

**Choice:** (a).

**Rationale:** The check tests what an installer gets, so a red result is a defect of a published version, and it is handled like any other defect: a fix commit and a new version. Per case, what a red means:

- An attestation or the SPDX asset missing: a provenance gap. Installs by tag are unaffected, because the chart pulls by tag unless `image.digest` is set. The finding is recorded and the release job is re-run.
- The chart missing from the index after the wait cap: the release job or GitHub Pages did not publish it. `helm install --version <v>` fails for everyone until it is published. The job's wait step names this case.
- The installation or a scenario fails with the artifacts intact: a defect of that version. Fix forward.
- Infrastructure (a Docker Hub rate limit, the kind cluster does not start, a lost runner): `gh run rerun <id> --failed`; no product change.

Each step of the job has its own name, so the reader sees the case without opening the matrix report. The owner's rule for the long legs (a red leg is a finding, not a blocker, 2026-11-01) gives the same answer for a check that runs after the release is public.

The development agent would revisit this at the first stable release, from which reliability and compatibility come first, and whenever a red check shows that a broken version reached users before its fix. Then option (b) for the index alone (a re-index without the version) is a decision of its own.

**Applied:** R-HA-047 (post-release check). The job `smoke-published`, its scripts and the case table of releasing.md (removed, Q-HA-281) carry it.

### Q-HA-164 · The post-release check is a job of `Release Docker & Helm`, and a dispatch runs only that job

**Superseded by [Q-HA-281](#q-ha-281--tests-run-before-a-release-not-after-it) (owner, 2026-11-10): there is no post-release check.**

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A job `smoke-published` in [build.yml](../../.github/workflows/build.yml) with `needs: [build, release-helm-gh]`; a `workflow_dispatch` input `version`; the publish jobs run on `release` events only, and the check runs after both succeed on a release and alone on a dispatch (chosen) | One run per release holds the publish jobs and the check; GitHub enforces the order | The release procedure already reaches a failed job of this workflow (`gh run rerun <id> --failed`) | The publish jobs need an `if:` gate; without it a dispatch on a branch would rebuild `latest` from that branch and force-push `gh-pages` |
| (b) A separate workflow file on `workflow_run` of `Release Docker & Helm` (completed, successful) and its own `workflow_dispatch` | The check cannot change a publish job, by construction | No gate to keep correct | The check is a second run; the query of the release flow (`gh run list --workflow "Release Docker & Helm"`) does not show its red |
| (c) A step in `release-helm-gh` before its push | Runs in the same job as the publish | None that the others lack | The artifacts it would check do not exist yet, so it would test the candidate, not what is published |

**Choice:** (a). The gate is the condition on each publish job, `if: github.event_name == 'release'`, and the check's condition is `!cancelled() && (github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' || (needs.build.result == 'success' && needs.release-helm-gh.result == 'success'))`. `!cancelled()` and not `always()`: a cancelled run stops the check, while the skipped publish jobs of a dispatch still let it run.

**Rationale:** Option (a) keeps the order and the evidence of a release in one run, and it gives the dispatch the one thing the release lacks: a way to run the check on a published version without cutting a release. The dispatch can reach any branch that the user can push to, and the workflow file of that branch runs with `DOCKERHUB_PAT`; that is the exposure [H-80](#h-80--self-hosted-runners-build-the-code-of-every-pull-request) already records for pushes, and a dispatch adds no reader beyond it. The `version` input is checked against `^v?[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$` in the job's first step, and against an existing release (`gh release view`) before anything is pulled. A test parses build.yml and fails when a publish job lacks its gate (R-HA-047), because the gate is what keeps a dispatch from publishing. The development agent would revisit this when the publish jobs need a rebuild on demand, which would move the check to (b) or give the publish jobs a gated input of their own.

A dispatch checks out the ref it was started on, and a release checks out its tag: the harness and the dev profile come from that checkout, the chart and the image from the release the input names. A dispatch on `main` for an older release therefore runs today's harness and dev values against that release's chart; an older chart that rejects a value of today's dev profile fails the install, which is a finding about the skew, not about the release.

Token permissions follow the same split. The workflow default is `contents: read`; `build` and `release-helm-gh` hold `contents: write` and nothing else (the release assets and the push of `gh-pages`; the workflow used to grant `id-token`, `actions` and `attestations` too, none of which a step uses), `release-helm-gh` also keeps `pages: write`: `contents: write` already pushes `gh-pages`, so dropping `pages` gains no least privilege, and whether GitHub's Pages build runs for a push with a `GITHUB_TOKEN` without it is not verified here. `smoke-published` holds `contents: read`. The release tag is checked against `^v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$` in both publish jobs before it reaches `sed`, and the dispatch input is never echoed. The edge of the check listens on host port 8101.

**Applied:** R-HA-047 (post-release check bullet). [build.yml](../../.github/workflows/build.yml) carries the gates, the permissions and the job; `deploy/dev/release-smoke.sh`, `deploy/dev/up.sh`, `deploy/dev/e2e.sh` (which refuses the set `release-smoke` without both `QUADER_RELEASE_*` variables) and the Makefile carry the rest; `TestR_HA_047_ADispatchRunsOnlyThePostReleaseCheck` and `TestR_HA_047_TheTokensHoldWhatTheJobsUse` guard the gates and the permissions (the test pins `pages: write` on `release-helm-gh`).

### Q-HA-165 · The smoke scenarios of E5.8 are the E2.1 matrix and the client smoke test

**Superseded by [Q-HA-281](#q-ha-281--tests-run-before-a-release-not-after-it) (owner, 2026-11-10): there is no post-release check.**

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The whole `npm` set, `TestNPM(Clients\|Matrix\|Replicas\|Collapse\|Upstream\|Endpoint\|Project)`, which the job `e2e-npm` runs for each change (E2.1 to E2.12) | Every npm criterion on the published artifacts | The widest evidence for the artifact | Repeats E2.2 to E2.12 on code that the change's run has already passed, once per release; the wall time of the set on a large runner is not measured here |
| (b) `TestNPMMatrix` (every scenario of R-NPM-045 for the eight gate rows of E2.1) and `TestNPMClients` (every row runs its client's `--version`, and the base URL reaches the cluster with a verified certificate) (chosen) | The criterion the roadmap names, and the client smoke test that precedes it | The matrix is the only test that installs and uses packages with every gate row, which is what an installer does; both tests exist | The matrix's wall time is not measured here; it is the first thing the first runs of the job show |
| (c) `TestNPMClients` alone | The smallest run | It exists | It shows that the clients start and reach the cluster, not that a package can be published and installed |
| (d) A new short scenario for the check: `helm install`, `/-/ping`, one `npm ci` per row | A small, fast check | Short | A criterion nobody has specified; it would need its own requirement |

**Choice:** (b). The Valkey-stopped variant (`TestNPMClosing`, the closing run of Q-NPM-46) is not in the check, because the check does not stop Valkey.

**Rationale:** E2.1 is the matrix, so the roadmap's words "E2.1's smoke scenarios" name it without a new definition. The check reruns no criterion of E2.2 to E2.12, whose code and cluster the change's run has already covered; the artifact is what differs, and the matrix is the test of an artifact's use. The development agent would revisit this when the first runs show that the matrix does not fit the job's time budget (120 minutes), or when a published-only failure appears in a criterion outside E2.1, which would justify option (a) for that criterion.

**Applied:** R-HA-047 (post-release check bullet and acceptance criterion); the set `release-smoke` of `deploy/dev/e2e.sh` (`TestNPM(Clients|Matrix)`).

### Q-HA-166 · The SBOM attestation of the image comes from a generator that runs the pinned syft

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough. The decision on the attestation stands; the SPDX file of the release, which this decision named as the asset of anchore/sbom-action, is written by the pinned image since [Q-HA-204](#q-ha-204--the-spdx-file-of-the-release-is-written-by-the-pinned-syft-image-from-the-registry-tag).

The release carried two syft versions: BuildKit's bundled scanner wrote the SBOM attestation of the image index with syft v1.51.0 (the SPDX creators of the `0.25.0` attestation name `Tool: syft-v1.51.0` and `Tool: buildkit-v0.34.2`), and anchore/sbom-action wrote the SPDX file of the release with `SYFT_VERSION`, v1.55.0. Evidence for the options:

- The scanner image of BuildKit, `docker/buildkit-syft-scanner`, has tags up to `1.12.1` (and `1`, `1.12`, `latest`, `stable-1`, `edge`). The `go.mod` of its tags `v1.10.0`, `v1.11.0`, `v1.12.0` and `v1.12.1` and of its `master` branch require syft v1.40.0, v1.42.3, v1.51.0, v1.51.0 and v1.51.0 (read with the GitHub API on 2026-11-07). The newest syft release is v1.57.0, and `SYFT_VERSION` is v1.55.0, so no scanner image carries the pinned version.
- BuildKit accepts any image that follows its scanner protocol as the generator (`sbom: generator=<image>`).

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) BuildKit's bundled scanner (`sbom: true`) and the version of the SPDX file follows it | The pin `SYFT_VERSION` moves to the scanner's syft | No new image | The version comes from the BuildKit version that buildx selects, not from a pin; the repository's rule is the newer version everywhere, and v1.51.0 is the older one |
| (b) `docker/buildkit-syft-scanner` at its newest tag, `SYFT_VERSION` lowered to v1.51.0 | One version, explicit | No new image | The older version everywhere; Renovate's bump of `SYFT_VERSION` would then need a scanner release first |
| (c) A generator image built from `SYFT_IMAGE` (`anchore/syft:$SYFT_VERSION` by digest) and a shell, built in the `build` job and served from a throwaway registry container on Docker's default bridge network, reached by its IP (chosen) | The attestation is written by the binary of the pin; the version appears once, in [versions.env](../../tools/versions.env) | One version; the generator is never published | A small scanner script of the repository ([scan.sh](../../tools/sbom-generator/scan.sh)) that follows BuildKit's protocol, and a registry container per release build |
| (d) The same generator pushed to Docker Hub as a published image | The same as (c), without the registry container | No registry step | A second published artifact of the organisation, which needs an owner decision on its repository, retention and who may pull it |
| (e) Option (c) with the registry on the runner's loopback and the builder in the host's network namespace (`network=host`) | The registry is reached as `localhost` | Fewer moving parts | Every `RUN` step of the image build, `npm ci` install scripts included, would share the runner pod's network namespace with whatever listens on its loopback |
| (f) Option (c) with the registry and the builder on a docker network of the run (`driver-opts: network=<name>`; the first build of this decision, merged and released as v0.25.1) | The registry is reached by its container name | The build steps neither share the runner's namespace nor the default bridge | The builder's resolver is Docker's embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11, which the network namespaces of BuildKit's `RUN` steps cannot use: every `RUN` step that needs a name failed (`RUN go mod download`: `lookup proxy.golang.org: i/o timeout`, both platforms, Release Docker & Helm run 42433259845). The pre-release job passed because its test image had no `RUN` step |

**Choice:** (c). The Containerfile takes `SYFT_IMAGE` and the shell image as build arguments without a default. `tools/sbom-generator/registry.sh start` starts the registry container `quader-sbom-registry-<run id>-<attempt>` on the default bridge network, publishes no port and prints its address, `<container IP>:5000`. The buildx builder (`docker/setup-buildx-action`, no `driver-opts`, so on the default bridge like every builder before this change) is created with a `buildkitd-config-inline` that allows plain HTTP for that one address. `registry.sh up` builds the generator for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`, pushes it and prints the reference by digest (`--metadata-file`, `containerimage.digest`); the build step passes `sbom: generator=<registry>:5000/sbom-generator@sha256:…`. A failed `up` removes the registry; the job removes the registry afterwards, and the builder is removed by `docker/setup-buildx-action`. The pin of the syft image is a digest, `SYFT_IMAGE=docker.io/anchore/syft:v1.55.0@sha256:…`. The version therefore appears twice in versions.env (`SYFT_VERSION` and the tag of `SYFT_IMAGE`); `check-pins.sh` holds the two equal, and a Renovate group rule (`syft`, like the k6 group) moves both in one pull request.

**Rationale:** The rule of the repository is one version of a tool; the newer one is the pin, and the scanner images lag it by several releases. The scanner protocol is the supported extension point, so the change adds no patch to BuildKit and no second SBOM tool: the generator is `syft scan dir:<rootfs>` plus the in-toto wrapper that BuildKit expects. The default bridge keeps option (e)'s exposure out of the build (the `RUN` steps do not share the runner's namespace) and gives the `RUN` steps the daemon's resolvers, which option (f) did not. The containers that can reach the registry are those on the bridge: the builder, the `RUN` steps of the image's own build and whatever else the daemon runs; none of them can replace what the builder runs, because the generator is referenced by digest, so who else reaches the registry is irrelevant; the reference by digest means that what the builder runs is the image the step just built, not a tag that something else on the network could have replaced. Checked with `make sbom-generator-check` on Docker Desktop: the generator builds, the builder reaches the registry by its IP over plain HTTP, a two-platform test image written with `--output type=oci` carries two SPDX attestations that name `Tool: syft-1.55.0`, and the registry and the builder are gone afterwards. The test image has a `RUN` step that resolves `proxy.golang.org`, the name the release build needs first, so a builder whose `RUN` steps cannot resolve names fails the pre-release job and not a release. The first run of option (f) did not have it; v0.25.1 exists on GitHub without image and chart, and the fix commit cuts the next version.

Three checks keep the version in one place. `make versions-check` runs [check-pins.sh](../../tools/sbom-generator/check-pins.sh): it fails when `SYFT_IMAGE` is not the digest form of `SYFT_VERSION`, when the Containerfile declares a default or names a syft image of its own, when any file of the repository outside versions.env names one (`anchore/syft:` or `anchore/syft@sha256:`), when build.yml reads a syft version other than `env.SYFT_VERSION` or sets `sbom` to anything but the generator, and when a `syft` on `PATH` is not the pin. The job `sbom-generator` of Test and Release runs the check above on every push and pull request and is a need of Semantic Release, so a syft bump that breaks the generator breaks that run and never a release. And the `build` job asserts, after the push, that both platforms' SBOM attestations name `syft-${SYFT_VERSION#v}` ([creators.sh](../../tools/sbom-generator/creators.sh)).

That last assertion can run only after the push, because BuildKit writes the attestations with the image. So the image is pushed by digest without a tag (`outputs: type=image,push-by-digest=true,name-canonical=true,push=true`), the assertion reads the digest, and only then does `docker buildx imagetools create -t … <repo>@<digest>` add the tags of docker/metadata-action (version, major.minor, major, sha, and `latest` on main). The attestation manifests are part of the pushed index, and the tags resolve to the same digest; checked on 2026-11-08 on a two-platform test image (the digest of the tag equals the pushed digest, the index keeps its four manifests, the SBOM creators and the provenance read through the tag). A failed assertion therefore moves no tag, publishes no chart and attaches no SPDX file: an untagged image by digest remains in the repository, which nothing resolves. The pre-release job still exists so that a release does not fail there. Not verified: a run of the `build` job itself, which needs a release (the first one after this change runs it), and that the runner's Docker daemon supports user-defined networks with container-name resolution for the buildx builder (it holds on Docker Desktop). The post-release check records the SBOM creators of the release it checks and does not assert them, because it also checks releases from before the change.

The development agent would revisit this when `docker/buildkit-syft-scanner` ships the pinned version (then (a) with `generator=docker/buildkit-syft-scanner:<tag>@sha256:…` drops the repository's script), or when the organisation wants the generator published (option (d)).

**Applied:** R-HA-047 (attestations bullet); [build.yml](../../.github/workflows/build.yml) (job `build`), [release.yml](../../.github/workflows/release.yml) (job `sbom-generator`), `tools/sbom-generator/`, [versions.env](../../tools/versions.env) (`SYFT_IMAGE`, `SBOM_GENERATOR_SHELL_IMAGE`, `SBOM_GENERATOR_REGISTRY_IMAGE`), the Makefile targets `versions-check` and `sbom-generator-check`, [releasing.md](../developer/releasing.md#the-release-pipeline); `TestR_HA_047_TheImageAttestationUsesThePinnedSyft` guards the build step and `TestR_HA_047_TheTokensHoldWhatTheJobsUse` the absence of any network option on the builder.

### Q-HA-170 · A variant drain evicts the release's pods and the variant's dependency by their own selectors in parallel drains, and nothing else on the node

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: R-HA-059's acceptance test evicts only the release's pods "except where a variant says otherwise", and `drain.sh <node>`
drains with the release's selector (Q-HA-68, Test and Release run 42406831768). Variants B, C and D each add one dependency. On the
three worker nodes of the dev profile a node also holds a Sentinel, often a Valkey data pod, a PostgreSQL instance or a pooler
instance, and sometimes an operator; SeaweedFS, the edge, the test upstreams and the client pods run on the control-plane node, which
no test drains. Nothing drains a variant's dependency today: the vulnerability tests and the npm tests run A only.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) `kubectl drain` without a selector | The node emptied as a node-pool upgrade empties it | The real drain | Evicts the PostgreSQL standby on a node of A, B or D (the commit stall of Q-HA-68), the operators and every dependency at once, so a variant no longer isolates the dependency it names |
| (b) Label the chosen pods and drain by the label | One `kubectl drain` | One process | Writes labels on pods that the Valkey and CloudNativePG operators own |
| (c) One `kubectl drain --pod-selector` per selector, started together (chosen) | The release's selector and the dependency's: for B the Valkey resource's data and Sentinel pods, for C the instances of the cluster `quader-db`, for D the pods of the two `Pooler` resources | Each run cordons, evicts and retries what a PodDisruptionBudget refuses, as `kubectl drain` does; nothing but the node is written | Several processes; the selectors are the operators' labels, read from the cluster when the script is written |

**Choice:** (c). `drain.sh [--also valkey|postgres|pooler]… <node>` returns when every run returned, the release's Deployments rolled
out, the node is uncordoned and the evicted dependency is whole: two Valkey data pods and three Sentinels ready, two ready
PostgreSQL instances, both poolers rolled out. The harness `test/e2e/drain_variants_test.go` picks the node of a variant, moves a
primary that is in the way first (as `drainNodeVariantA`), runs the drain as the caller's fault and judges the variant's own
condition with R-HA-059's `SIGKILL`, `Pending` and duration conditions; the load or the probes are the caller's, so E5.9 runs the same
harness under the full load and the blocks of E5.13 under their probes.

**Rationale:** each variant names one dependency, and draining only that one keeps a failure attributable to it. The development
agent would revisit it if the dev profile gets more worker nodes than dependencies, where (a) would evict nothing a variant does not
name.

**Applied:** R-HA-059 (how the test drains variants B to E); `deploy/dev/drain.sh`, `test/e2e/drain_variants_test.go`.

### Q-HA-171 · Variant B evicts the Valkey primary without a planned failover, and its counter condition covers the replicas that ran through the drain

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: rule 5 says "Running `SENTINEL FAILOVER` before the primary stops shortens that window"; B's condition is that
`quader_valkey_primary_changes_total` rises on every replica and no replica turns unready. The drain evicts the node's Quader pods at
the same time, and a replacement may start before or after Sentinel promotes the replica.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Evict the primary as the drain reaches it; judge the counter and the readiness on every replica that ran before the drain and was not evicted (chosen) | Sentinel fails over after `down-after-milliseconds`, Quader runs degraded meanwhile (R-HA-057); a replacement must be ready at the end, its counter is logged | The drain of a platform without a pre-stop failover, the harder path; the condition is judged where it can hold | A replacement that saw the change is not required to |
| (b) `SENTINEL FAILOVER` first, then drain | The recommended procedure | The shortest degraded window | The eviction then meets a replica: it is the planned failover the failover rows already run (`TestNPMHA`, Q-VULN-88) |
| (c) Every replica, replacements included | The sentence read literally | — | A replacement that starts after the promotion can never see a change, so the condition would fail on timing |

**Choice:** (a). "Rises" is at least one; the planned failover's "exactly one" of `TestNPMHA` stays there. Readiness is the monitor of
the failover tests (`/readyz` of every replica once a second), judged for the replicas that ran through.

**Rationale:** the variant proves the drain of the primary's node, which the planned failover does not. The development agent would
revisit it when the Valkey operator fails a primary over before it stops: then (a) and (b) are one drain.

**Applied:** R-HA-059 (how the test drains variants B to E); `test/e2e/drain_variants_test.go`. Q-HA-181 adds what the first runs
did not know: the failover of this variant is not reliable on its own, and the test keeps the primary lost until it has happened.

### Q-HA-172 · Variant C lets CloudNativePG request the switchover at the cordon, evicts the old primary, and reads the order from the cluster's own timestamps

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: C's condition is that CloudNativePG acts before the eviction. The operator switches a primary away from a cordoned
node by itself (F-65, Q-HA-126): it requests the switchover (`.status.targetPrimary` names another instance, with `targetPrimaryTimestamp`)
and marks the old primary's `instanceRole` `unhealthy` while target and current primary differ, which the PodDisruptionBudgets of the
primary and of the replicas select neither of, so the eviction is admitted from the request on, not from the completion (read in the
CloudNativePG 1.30 sources of the module cache: `cluster_controller.go`, `replicas.go`, `pkg/specs/poddisruptionbudget.go`). The evicted
instance keeps a volume bound to its node (kind's local-path storage), so it waits for the uncordon. The dev profile runs two
instances with `dataDurability: preferred`.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The order from Kubernetes events | The eviction event against an event of the operator | No poller | The switchover is a status change; events are pruned and not a contract of the operator |
| (b) `.status.targetPrimary` with its `targetPrimaryTimestamp`, and the time the old primary pod's deletion was requested (its `deletionTimestamp` minus its grace period, which is the end of the grace period), both the server's own, read by a poll every 250 ms from before the drain (chosen) | Passes when the switchover was requested before the pod's deletion was requested (a second of resolution allowed); it fails when the eviction comes first or no switchover is requested | Read where the operator and the API server write them; independent of the poll's resolution | The request, not the completion: the new primary is promoted a few seconds later, which the probes judge as zero failed requests |
| (c) `failover.sh` first, then drain | A switchover the test asks for | Deterministic | Not variant C: the eviction meets a standby, as variant A's moves do |

**Choice:** (b). `drain.sh --also postgres` waits for two ready instances after the uncordon, before the next fault. The stall of
commits while the operator drops the drained synchronous standby (Q-HA-68) belongs to this variant on the dev profile.

**Rationale:** (b) judges the operator's own order of steps as far as it guarantees one: the request precedes the eviction. A stricter order (the completion first) is not what the operator promises, and the probes carry the traffic condition. Variant C's condition in R-HA-059 is worded that way. The development agent would revisit the
profile when E5.9's variant C under the full load meets the stall: rule 5 asks for three instances with `dataDurability: required`.

**Applied:** R-HA-059 (how the test drains variants B to E; the variant table row C and rule 5's PostgreSQL row); `deploy/dev/drain.sh`, `test/e2e/drain_variants_test.go`.

### Q-HA-173 · The pooler profile of the dev cluster carries rule 5's drain prerequisites, with lifetimes shortened for the test

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: rule 5 asks of a pooler instance two instances on different nodes, a PodDisruptionBudget, PgBouncer 1.23 or later and a
stop that outwaits Quader's pooled connections; R-HA-058 recommends `max_conn_lifetime: 5m` with `1m` of jitter.
`deploy/dev/pooler.yaml` (M0) had two instances per pooler and nothing else; `values-pooler.yaml` set no lifetime and declared
`server_connections: 24`, where the two poolers hold 2 × 20 + 2 × 4 = 48 server connections; the dev database set no role
defaults, which preflight requires on a pooled connection (`checkRoleDefaults` in `internal/meta/postgres/preflight.go`). No set had
run the profile. Running it showed four more facts: the pooler presents the cluster's server certificate, which named only the
`quader-db-rw`, `-r` and `-ro` Services (`verify-full` failed); the CloudNativePG pooler manager turns `SIGTERM` into `SIGINT`, so
the instance exits within a second whatever the grace period (the first run of variant D saw two `500`s at the eviction); pgxpool
closes an idle connection past its lifetime only in its health check; and every `jsonb` parameter failed in exec mode
([Q-ARCH-348](architecture.md#q-arch-348--jsonb-parameters-are-jsonrawmessage-so-that-exec-mode-sends-them-as-text)).

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The spec's example: lifetime 5m with 1m of jitter, sleep 400 s, grace 460 s | As production would run it | The recommended values | A pooler pod's drain takes about 6.5 minutes, the variant about 8 |
| (b) Lifetime 60 s with 15 s of jitter, `health_check_period: 5s`, a `preStop` sleep of 90 s, grace 120 s, a PodDisruptionBudget with `maxUnavailable: 1` per pooler, a hostname spread with `DoNotSchedule` and `nodeTaintsPolicy: Honor`, role defaults set by `up.sh`, the pooler Services in `certificates.serverAltDNSNames`, `server_connections: 48` (chosen) | Rule 5 holds: the last connection is gone after at most 60 + 15 + 5 = 80 s, 10 s before the sleep ends | A drain of a pooler pod takes 90 s; connections are opened again every minute; the dev values are not the recommended ones |
| (c) A grace period only, as the first reading of rule 5 | The profile as planned | Nothing to add to the Pooler | The instance exits within a second: it tests a lost instance (R-HA-052's pooler row), not a drain |
| (d) No lifetime | Quader keeps its connections and the pooler pod is killed at the end of its grace | — | Same as (c) |

**Choice:** (b). The role defaults are the configuration's defaults (`internal/config/database.go`): `statement_timeout` 30s,
`lock_timeout` 5s, `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` 60s, `client_connection_check_interval` 1s (Q-ARCH-1041 of
[architecture.md](architecture.md)) and `search_path` `quader`, set by `up.sh` with
`ALTER ROLE quader IN DATABASE quader SET …` when `QUADER_POOLER=1`. The facts read from the cluster: PgBouncer 1.25.2 in CloudNativePG
1.30's pooler image; the pooler's certificate names only the cluster's Services, so `deploy/dev/postgres.yaml` adds the pooler
Services to `certificates.serverAltDNSNames` (a pooler started before the change presents the old certificate until it restarts);
preflight refuses to start without the role defaults, naming the login and the setting.

**Rationale:** the variant judges the drain rule: the stop must outwait Quader's connections, which a sleep with the pod out of its
Service does and the grace period does not. R-HA-058 states the rule and the arithmetic for operators. The shorter lifetime keeps the
nightly leg short. The development agent would revisit it when CloudNativePG's manager waits for clients on `SIGTERM`: the sleep
would then be dropped from the profile and the rule.

**Applied:** R-HA-058 ("The pooler is highly available", the example), R-HA-059 rule 5 and its table row; `deploy/dev/pooler.yaml`,
`values-pooler.yaml`, `postgres.yaml`, `up.sh`; [local-profile.md](../developer/local-profile.md); the README's `database.pooler`
reference and [the admin configuration page](../manual/admin/configuration.md).

### Q-HA-174 · Variant E places its backup pod on the drained node through a preferred node affinity

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: E's condition is that the backup Job completes and the eviction is not counted against `backoffLimit`. `TestBackupDrain`
pins its backup pod with a `nodeSelector`, so the pod that replaces it waits for the uncordon; R-HA-059 fails a Quader pod that stays
`Pending` for more than 60 s, and the backup CronJob has no scheduling values.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A `nodeSelector`, as `TestBackupDrain` | The Job's pods run on that node only | As built | The replacement pod is `Pending` until the uncordon, about the length of the rollouts, and the pod watch counts it |
| (b) Cordon the other nodes while the Job starts | As `TestBackupDrain` steers the restore Job | No change to the Job | Writes on two other nodes while the cluster serves; a pod rescheduled in that moment lands on the drained node |
| (c) A preferred node affinity of weight 100 for the node (chosen) | The scheduler puts the first pod there when it fits (the harness checks and starts the Job again otherwise); the replacement runs wherever it fits | The replacement starts at once | One more field of the test's Job description |

**Choice:** (c). The Job runs with `backoffLimit: 0` into a fresh target prefix at `QUADER_BACKUP_COPY_BYTES_PER_SECOND=512KiB` over at
least 16 MiB of files the harness puts first, so that the copy outlasts the 20 s before the drain (the eviction restarts the copy of
the whole installation in the next pod, so 256 KiB/s took 16 minutes on a cluster that had run the vulnerability tests); it must end
`Complete` with at least two pods within 15 minutes.

**Rationale:** (c) is the only option under which the replacement is scheduled as in production. The development agent would revisit
it if the chart gets scheduling values for the backup CronJob.

**Applied:** R-HA-059 (how the test drains variants B to E); `test/e2e/backup_env_test.go` (`bakJob`), `test/e2e/drain_variants_test.go`.

### Q-HA-180 · A replay handler starts follow-up work by writing a job row in its own transaction

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: F-72. A replayed `repository.narrowed` can switch a repository's scanning on or widen the advisories it matches
([repositories-and-proxy.md](repositories-and-proxy.md) R-REPO-061). The setting alone blocks nothing until the repository's
versions are evaluated again (R-VULN-011). After a Quader backup restore the first complete import evaluates every stored version,
because the advisory tables are `transient`; after a point-in-time restore the advisory tables come back and nothing triggers an
evaluation. A handler is registered at start-up and gets only the transaction and `journal.Env` (`internal/journal/replay.go`); the
restore commands build no job registry (`cmd/quader/backup_restore.go`, `admin_postrestore.go`).

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) `journal.Env` carries a job queue that both restore commands build | The handler calls `Enqueue` | The queue's own path | Both commands need the composition root's job registry; one more member of the shared `Env` for one handler |
| (b) The handler writes the job row itself, with the kind's spec from the owning package (chosen) | `jobs.EnqueueTx(ctx, tx, spec, e)`: the queue's insert without the registry lookup and without the wake-up signal; `vuln.RescanKindSpec()` is the spec that the application registers too | No change of the shared journal contract or of the commands; the job exists exactly when the entry's change commits; the workers that start after the restore pick it up | The spec of the kind is read from the owning package instead of the registry, so both places must use the one function |
| (c) No follow-up; rely on the next full evaluation | — | Nothing to build | After a point-in-time restore the strengthened setting blocks nothing until an advisory changes: fails open |

**Choice:** (b). The application registers the rescan with `vuln.RescanKindSpec()` plus its handler, so the spec has one source.
**Rationale:** the follow-up belongs to the change that needs it, in its transaction, as every enqueue of Quader does (R-ARCH-016);
the restore commands stay free of the worker wiring. The development agent would revisit (a) when a second handler needs a job.
**Applied:** R-HA-054 "Replay rules"; R-REPO-061 step 7; `internal/jobs/queue.go`, `internal/vuln/jobs.go`,
`internal/app/wire_vuln_eval.go`.

### Q-HA-181 · Variant B keeps the evicted Valkey primary lost until the Sentinels name another one, and asks for the failover when they do not

Status: Decided by the development agent — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: F-78. Variant B's condition is that `quader_valkey_primary_changes_total` rises on every replica that ran through the drain
(Q-HA-171), which needs a failover. In one of three runs on kind (2026-11-08) the counter stayed at 0. The first suspicion was that
the evicted primary, which has no volume claim, returns under its own name within `down-after-milliseconds` (5 s) and no Sentinel
sees it down. Measured on the dev cluster, 14 drains of the Valkey pods alone from the node of the primary (the Sentinels and data
pods only, `kubectl drain --pod-selector`; the event excerpts of the two drains without a sidecar request are below) and the variant itself:

- The Valkey operator's sidecar (`internal/sidecar/drain.go` of the operator) asks a Sentinel for `SENTINEL FAILOVER` when its
  `SIGTERM` finds Valkey still answering `INFO replication`; Valkey itself waits for its replica before it exits, about 0.3 s. In 12 of
  14 drains a failover was requested (in one the first Sentinel, itself being evicted, refused and the second accepted) and the Sentinels
  named the other pod 1.2 to 6.2 s after Valkey's `SIGTERM` (1.2 s in seven). In 2 the sidecar's `INFO` failed (connection refused;
  `AUTH failed ... connection reset by peer` during Valkey's shutdown) and it exited without a request.
- Without the request the Sentinels fail over by themselves. In one of the two, `+sdown master` came 5.2 s after Valkey's `SIGTERM`,
  `+odown` 0.4 s later and the new primary was named 6.5 s after it. In the other (the drain that reproduced F-78) the sidecar's
  signal came 6.5 s after Valkey's, the Sentinel on the drained node was gone, and the two that remained both started a failover
  (`+try-failover` 1.3 s apart); neither was elected and both logged `-failover-abort-not-elected` 10 s later, with `Next failover delay:
  I will not start a failover before` two minutes ahead (twice the `failover-timeout` of 60 s). The primary was down for about 55 s,
  came back empty and was named primary again, and the counter stayed at 0. The return within 5 s was not the cause.
<details>
<summary>Sentinel events of the two drains in which the sidecar made no failover request (times are UTC; the first Sentinel of each file was evicted with the primary or left out)</summary>

```text
## it-9
valkey SIGTERM 10:11:47.759
10:11:54.309  sidecar: signal received, starting graceful drain
10:11:54.311  sidecar drain: failed to detect role during drain, exiting immediately {"
s1: 10:11:54.013 # +sdown master quader-valkey valkey-0 16379
s1: 10:11:56.418 # +odown master quader-valkey valkey-0 16379 #quorum 2/2
s1: 10:11:56.418 # +try-failover master quader-valkey valkey-0 16379
```

Drain 9 is the one without a failover: both remaining Sentinels reach `+odown` and `+try-failover`, both abort 10 s later and set the
two-minute delay; the primary returned at 10:12:43 and `-odown` followed. Drain 11 recovered through the Sentinels' own election.
In the 12 drains with a request, `+try-failover` followed the sidecar's request within 0.1 s and `+switch-master` within 1.2 to 6.2 s of
Valkey's `SIGTERM`.

</details>

- `down-after-milliseconds` and `failover-timeout` are not fields of the Valkey resource (the operator renders 5000 and 60000), so
  the profile cannot shorten them.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The test keeps the evicted primary lost until a Sentinel names another one, and sends `SENTINEL FAILOVER` when none has 25 s after the eviction (chosen) | A finalizer on the primary's pod, set before `drain.sh`: the StatefulSet cannot create the pod of that name before the object is gone. The test removes it when `sentinelPrimary` names another pod; after 25 s without that it runs `SENTINEL FAILOVER` (which Sentinel runs without the two-minute delay) and logs it; after 90 s without a failover the variant fails | The disturbance is fixed: the primary is lost and a failover follows, whichever of the platform's paths takes it; the pass condition stays what R-HA-059 says; the platform's race is in the log | The command is the test's help in the one case the Sentinels did not manage; the test does not judge the operator or Sentinel |
| (b) The hold alone, no command | The same finalizer, the failover left to the platform | Nothing is sent by the test | The split vote leaves the variant red for 90 s and again at every occurrence, on a property of Sentinel and the operator that Quader does not own and variant B does not test |
| (c) Shorter `down-after-milliseconds` in the dev profile | Fewer seconds before a Sentinel acts | Looks like the cheapest | Not configurable (above), and it would change neither the sidecar's miss nor the split vote |
| (d) `SENTINEL FAILOVER` before the eviction | Q-HA-171 (b) | Deterministic | Not variant B: the eviction then meets a replica |
| (e) Accept a counter of 0 when the primary came back | A weaker condition | Never red | The variant then proves nothing about Quader's handling of a primary change; refused |

**Choice:** (a). The assist is careful about what it starts: `SENTINEL FAILOVER` answers `-INPROG` per Sentinel, and a Sentinel that is
not leading would accept it and begin a new epoch, so before each attempt the test reads `SENTINEL MASTER` on every reachable Sentinel
and sends nothing while one lists `failover_in_progress`; it sends the command to the first Sentinel that answers and stops at its
answer. An accepted command that has not ended after 10 s (the election timeout) was aborted, and one more is sent; there are at most two.
Every attempt is logged, and when the assist fires the test prints a `::warning::` line for the nightly summary. All kubectl calls of
the hold have a 15 s bound, the release is retried for 30 s (only `NotFound` and `Precondition failed` are final), and `TestMain` removes
a stale hold finalizer from every pod of the namespace before the first test, so a killed run heals at the next start. The variant's conditions are unchanged: the counter rises by at least 1 on every replica that ran through, none turns
unready, and the Sentinels name another primary than before. The finalizer name is `e2e.quader.guided-traffic.com/hold-valkey-primary`;
`t.Cleanup` removes it, so a test that ends early leaves no pod `Terminating`.

**Rationale:** what the variant tests is Quader through the loss of its Valkey primary during a drain (R-HA-057, R-HA-059), and that
needs a primary that is lost and a failover that follows. The failover itself is the platform's: the operator's sidecar and the
Sentinels race, and the race is not Quader's to win. Fixing the disturbance rather than the assertion keeps the pass condition; the
log says when the Sentinels did not manage by themselves, so the platform's weakness is not hidden by the help. The weakness is a
finding of its own, for the Valkey operator: a sidecar that did not reach Valkey at `SIGTERM` could still ask for the failover
(it knows it was the primary), and two Sentinels that abort an election could retry before two `failover-timeout`. For an installation
it means a drained Valkey primary can leave Quader without a primary for up to two minutes, where it runs degraded (R-HA-057). The
development agent would revisit (b) when the operator closes both gaps, and (a) when the profile runs the Valkey pods on volume claims.

**What variant B no longer covers:** a primary that restarts at the same address within `down-after-milliseconds`, so that no
Sentinel ever sees it down and no failover happens. That case is real for a platform whose Valkey pods restart fast, and Quader's part
in it is that the replicas keep serving (R-HA-057) while the primary comes back empty and its replica resynchronizes to nothing; the
spec accepts the cost (cache only, R-HA-057 rule 2). `deploy/dev/valkey-kill.sh` names that outcome (`restarted in place`) and
accepts it as correct next to `moved`, so the failure suite passes either way; no test asserts the replicas' counter for the quick
return.

**The Valkey operator and a long-lived Terminating pod:** read in the operator's source, not exercised on the cluster. It tolerates
one: the rolling-update waits end the pass while a pod of the tier is Terminating, and only after the pod is 2 minutes past its
graceful deadline (the deletion timestamp, 75 s after the delete for a data pod) does it report the condition `PodTerminationStalled`
and carry on with the rest of the pass. The hold lasts 90 s at most, so it ends well before that. The five runs showed no other effect.
`kubectl drain` waits until the evicted pod is gone, so the test releases the hold while `drain.sh` runs and the drain time includes
the hold (33 to 54 s measured, 28 s without it).

**Applied:** R-HA-059 (how the test drains variants B to E; rule 5's Valkey row); R-HA-057 rule 8; the failure table; Q-HA-171 (a note); `test/e2e/drain_variants_hold_test.go`,
`test/e2e/drain_variants_test.go`; [e2e.md](../developer/e2e.md#variant-b-the-hold).


### Q-HA-230 · The transfer loop of the drain tests is a closed loop, so a stall of the edge cannot release a burst above the write class

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: F-119. The nightly dispatch 42578594755 ran the set `drain-roles` alone on the large runner class. Everything passed except the upload and download loop on `generic-local` (`TestDrainRoles`): 9 PUTs answered `429` and 7 answered `502`. Two hypotheses stood open: (a) a replica that turned ready decided the cluster-scoped `write` class in its fallback mode, with a share of the budget over the live replicas, because its Valkey client was not yet available; (b) the edge got a reset from a `packages` pod in its shutdown sequence.

Evidence (read from the artifacts of that run). **(a) is refuted.** The refused PUTs carry `RateLimit-Policy="write";q=50;w=5`; during a fallback the policy names the replica's share (`setRateLimitFields` in [ratelimit.go](../../internal/api/v1/ratelimit.go) prints `v.Limit`, which is `burst / n` with `n` replicas, 16 for three), so the answers were decided on the shared counters. The replicas that refused (`57mrv`, `bxxhp`, `fncjv`) logged `valkey available` at 07:43:40.963 and turned ready at 07:43:41.104, 0.14 s later. **(b) is refuted as a drain race.** The last eviction was at 07:45:22 and the refusals are from 07:50:42 to 07:50:45, five minutes later, when all replicas were replacements and none was shutting down. All 16 failures are 429s of the limiter: the three pods logged exactly 16 PUT answers of 429 for the principal `e2e-xfer`, and the edge's access lines show `502` with the flags `SH` (no response header from the server) for 7 of those same requests, matched by path and by the millisecond. **The cause is a stall.** From 07:50:08 until about 07:50:50 the whole cluster was slow: all eight `npm ci` loops took about 40 s instead of 7 s, the edge's connect time to the pods rose to its 5 s bound (`Tc` 4.9 to 5.0 s), the `packages` pods answered 400 to 1,000 requests per 5 s instead of 2,000 to 3,000, and the first refused PUT had waited 11.3 s. The loop starts its iterations on a clock (`constant-arrival-rate`, 4 a second), so the 40 iterations of ten stalled seconds all reached the pods when the stall ended: 36 PUTs in the second 07:50:43 alone, against the 50 per 5 s window (10 a second) of the write class for one principal. The limiter did what R-API-016 and R-ARCH-034 say; a refused request counts against the window, as the rule says, so the burst kept the loop refused for three more seconds. Verified: all of the above from the artifacts of run 42578594755. Not verified: what stalled the cluster at 07:50:08. The pod watch and the events that the test records show no pod event after the last replacement at 07:45:22, and the pods' logs show no restart or failover in that minute; the load of the runner itself was not measured.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Raise the write class in the dev profile | `api.rate_limits.write` in [values-dev.yaml](../../deploy/dev/values-dev.yaml) as the anonymous class already is | One line | `TestE1_08` relies on the default write class; the burst still has a bound, only a higher one |
| (b) Keep the open loop, widen what the test tolerates | Allow 429 in the transfer loop | None | A weaker pass condition: a 429 caused by a product limit would pass |
| (c) A closed loop (chosen) | `RATE` clients, each starting its next iteration when the last one ended and at the earliest one second after the last one started | A stall holds the clients; nothing piles up; the rate is at most `RATE` iterations a second, below the write class by construction (4 against 10); the pass condition is unchanged | The loop no longer keeps a rate through a stall (it did not keep it before either: the iterations only waited) |
| (d) Change the limiter so that held requests do not count | Charge a request to the window it was sent in | Would absorb a stall | The pod cannot know when the client sent it; Q-HA-66 already charges the window of arrival at the pod for what the pod itself held |

**Choice:** (c). [transfer.js](../../test/e2e/k6/transfer.js) runs `constant-vus` with `RATE` VUs, and every iteration ends with a sleep up to one second after its start, also after a failed PUT. The assertions of `TestDrainRoles` and `TestE14Drain` are not changed: no failed transfer, no wrong checksum.

**Rationale:** The defect was in the load, not in the product: an open loop turns every stall of the edge into a burst that a limiter must refuse, whatever a drain does. A closed loop is also the model of the clients the drain criterion is about (an `npm ci`, a `curl -T`, a CI job wait for the answer). Revisit when a run shows a 429 or a 502 for this loop that is not preceded by an edge stall, or when the stall of 07:50:08 recurs and is traced to the product. Verified after the change: two nightly dispatches of `drain-roles` on the branch (42584245924 and 42588838964, with other legs of the dispatch and of other dispatches on the large class at the same time) ran the transfer loop with 0 failures in 5,416 and 4,814 requests (slowest request 8.9 s and 6.8 s, so stalls of several seconds did occur and held the clients). Both runs failed on the p99 conditions of R-HA-059 (documents 1.64 s against a warm-up of 755 ms in the first, 5.25 s against 840 ms and all requests 13.8 s against 1.7 s in the second); those conditions are not the subject of this decision. Two observations stay open and are recorded in F-119: what stalled the cluster, and that an early 429 of a 256 KiB PUT reached the client as `502 SH` in 7 of 16 cases behind HAProxy Ingress. A plain TLS client against the real server (HTTP/1.1, 100 KiB to 1 MiB bodies, written fast or in 5 ms steps, the answer read concurrently or only after the write) got the 429 in every one of 320 attempts, so the loss is not reproduced and no product change is made for it.

**Applied:** [transfer.js](../../test/e2e/k6/transfer.js) (the executor and the pacing); [e2e.md](../developer/e2e.md) (the file table).

### Q-HA-288 · The rotation row of E0.15 loads the cluster with a closed loop, and the load loops of the e2e tests register their stop before they start

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: F-119 item 3. `TestE15TLS` (the certificate renewed under load, R-ARCH-035, R-HA-063) failed in Test and Release 42839263211 with 353 of 9,602 answers at status 0 (`context_canceled`), and earlier in 42818570044 with 7 of about 10,000 at `502`.

Evidence (artifacts of run 42839263211, per-second counts of `k6-rotate/console.log`, the edge's and the pods' logs). **The 353 are requests that nobody answered, cut off by the stop of the test.** Every one started between 91.6 s and 101.5 s of the load (15:15:46 to 15:15:56) and none of them has an answer. The 443 requests of that window (the 353 and the 90 that `parseK6` sets aside because they started in the last two seconds) are the whole last 10 s: the time between the moment the last pod served the new certificate and the end of the test's `time.Sleep(10 * time.Second)`, when `k.stop` sent SIGINT and k6 cancelled what was in flight. Up to 91.5 s every 5 s bucket has 500 requests and no failure (the slowest 2.0 s). The stall is cluster-wide: the edge logged 1 to 15 answers a second instead of about 55 from 15:15:46, the api pods 3 to 6 instead of 45 to 60, PostgreSQL logged statements of 60 to 290 ms, the api pods logged `valkey degraded` (`circuit_open` at 15:15:49, `probe_failed: context deadline exceeded` at 15:15:50), and k6 itself started 688 instead of 1,000 requests in the last 10 s. **The certificate is not the cause**: the last pod served the new certificate at 15:15:42, each web pod reloaded its listeners once per listener (`quader_tls_reloads_total` 0 to 2, errors 0), no pod restarted, neither edge pod reloaded HAProxy between 15:15:30 and 15:16:00 (its updates at 15:15:32 and 15:15:55 were endpoint slices), and the earlier recurrence (42618038153) had its 502s 35 s before the first reload. **The harness did not produce the status 0**: it ended requests that the stall had held for up to 10 s, and `parseK6` rightly counts those older than two seconds as failures. Not verified: what stalled the cluster at 15:15:46 (neither the artifacts nor the logs name it, and the load of the runner was not measured), and whether the open loop's 1,035 connections at the edge (`1035/1035` in the edge's access lines at steady state, from 2,000 pre-allocated VUs at 100 requests a second) contribute to it. The closed loop was run once on the local cluster; that run says nothing about the stall.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Widen the pass condition | Allow status 0, or set aside everything cancelled by the stop | Green | Hides a request that nobody answered for 10 s; rejected |
| (b) Keep the open loop for the row | No change | None | The load keeps its rate through a stall and releases a burst after it, and keeps up to 2,000 connections open, which adds to a stall of a shared runner |
| (c) A closed loop for the row (chosen) | `LOOP=closed` in [load.js](../../test/e2e/k6/load.js): 100 clients, each starts its next request one second after the last started or when it ended, with offsets spread over the first second | At most 100 requests and connections; a stall slows the load instead of piling it up; the pass condition and the 95 % rate bound are unchanged | A stall still shows: a request held for more than two seconds at the stop fails the row, as it should |
| (d) A closed loop for every user of `load.js` | One load shape | None for the failover and drain tests | They hold requests on purpose for up to `retry.max_elapsed` and expect the load to go on at its rate meanwhile; with a closed loop the held clients would fall under the 95 % bound |

**Choice:** (c), by `k6Opts.closed` and `startK6Closed` in [env_test.go](../../test/e2e/env_test.go); `TestE15TLS` uses it. The other users of `load.js` keep the open loop. The assertions of the row are not changed.

**Second part, the loops left behind.** A clients pod outlives the test, and a detached load loop (`setsid nohup sh ./loop.sh`) in it runs until its `stop` file appears. `startNPMLoad`, `startNuGetLoad` and `startNuGetLoops` registered the `t.Cleanup` that touches the stop files after they had started the loops and k6, so a test that failed in between (k6 not sending, a failed exec) left the loops running into the next scenario. The cleanup is now registered before the first loop starts. The infinite `curl` loops found on the local cluster (`while true; do curl … /system/ping` and `/system/replicas` against `quader-api:8080`, started in `quader-e2e-npm-0`) are not in any test of the repository or in its history: they come from a hand-run experiment script of an earlier session that started them with `kubectl exec` in the background and relied on `sleep 200; kill $(jobs -p)` inside the pod, which never ran when the exec session ended first. No test starts them, so no test change stops them.

**Rationale:** The defect is in the load shape, not in the product: a load that grows when the cluster slows measures the runner. Revisit when a run of the row shows a request unanswered for more than two seconds with the closed loop and no cluster-wide stall in the access lines, or when the stall at 15:15:46 is traced to the product or to the open loop's connections.

**Applied:** [load.js](../../test/e2e/k6/load.js), [env_test.go](../../test/e2e/env_test.go), [e15_tls_test.go](../../test/e2e/e15_tls_test.go), [npm_load_test.go](../../test/e2e/npm_load_test.go), [nuget_load_test.go](../../test/e2e/nuget_load_test.go), [upgrade_loops_test.go](../../test/e2e/upgrade_loops_test.go); [e2e.md](../developer/e2e.md) (the file table and E0.15).

### Q-HA-289 · The point-in-time drill and the dev stack's release install take over the replica counts that earlier tests set with kubectl

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: E5.1. The drill (`TestBackupPITR…`, set `backup-pitr`) called the one-off commands `quader admin storage restore-versions`, `quader admin maintenance pause-deletions` and `resume-deletions` for the first time on a cluster on 2026-11-10. Run 2 failed in step 1: `helm upgrade` stopped with `conflict with "kubectl" with subresource "scale" using apps/v1: .spec.replicas` on `quader-worker`, because Deployments of a cluster that earlier tests used carry `kubectl scale` as the field manager of `spec.replicas` (the tests of the set `alerts` and the mirror tests scale `quader-worker`). | Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) `--force-conflicts` on the drill's `helm upgrade` (chosen) | The drill's own release values win over a leftover field manager | The drill sets every role to zero, so it has to own the replica count; one flag, in the one helper `pitrHelm` | Hides a conflict on another field too; the drill's values are the profile's and should win there as well |
| (b) Remove the `kubectl scale` calls of the other tests | Those tests restore the count through helm | No flag | Many callers (`alerts_test.go`, `mirror_env_test.go`, shell scripts), and each cleanup is itself a `kubectl scale` |
| (c) Run the drill only on a fresh cluster | Document it | No change | The nightly job runs it after the `backup` set on the same cluster; local runs reuse clusters |

Not changed: the order of the cluster's plugin rollout and the first helm install in `up.sh` (a run started while the Cluster still restarts fails in the migration Job; CI starts from a fresh cluster and the set waits for it).
