### Q-HA-491 · A worktree's kind cluster, its edge port and its kubeconfig are its own

Status: **Decided by the development agent on 2026-11-23** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.
Extends [Q-HA-489](#q-ha-489--every-image-of-the-development-profiles-carries-the-checkouts-tag-and-the-charts-run-the-image-they-were-given)
from the image to the cluster.

Context: the image tag was the checkout's since Q-HA-489, the cluster `quader`, the edge port 8080 and the kubeconfig were not, so a
builder's worktree and the main checkout could not run a profile at once, and no builder ran the journey or end-to-end test it had
changed before it reported: a journey's new line made `e2e (vuln)` red on 2026-11-23 that only the pipeline could show.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Derived from the checkout: `quader-<worktree>` (`dev-tag.sh --cluster`), the port picked free by kind at creation (`hostPort` 0) and read back from the node, the kubeconfig `.dev/kubeconfig` of the worktree; the main checkout keeps `quader`, 8080 and the caller's kubeconfig (chosen) | `lib.sh`, `up.sh`, `cluster-logs.sh` | Unique by construction, nothing to claim or to give back; every script already read the port back from the node; the owner's and the pipeline's names stay | A worktree's port differs per cluster (the scripts print it) |
| (b) Numbered instances with a claim, as the UI profile's | A table of names and ports | Fixed ports per instance | A cluster outlives every process, so the claim is a file to clean up; a name derived from the checkout needs none |
| (c) Builders set the three variables by hand | Nothing to build | — | Two builders chose the same UI instance a minute apart on 2026-11-23; a default that collides is what made them meet |

**Choice:** (a). **Rationale:** a worktree's name is already unique on the machine and is what the image tag is made of; a port the kernel
picks cannot collide with another listener. The development agent would revisit it if a tool needs the edge on a known port in a
worktree, which `QUADER_DEV_HTTP_PORT` then sets.

**Applied in the spec:** none (development tooling). Code: [lib.sh](../../deploy/dev/lib.sh), [dev-tag.sh](../../deploy/dev/dev-tag.sh)
`--cluster`, [up.sh](../../deploy/dev/up.sh), [cluster-logs.sh](../../deploy/dev/cluster-logs.sh); held by
`TestDevProfileClusterPortAndKubeconfigArePerCheckout` ([checkoutprofiles_test.go](../../internal/tools/ciworkflows/checkoutprofiles_test.go)).
Elsewhere: [local-profile.md](../developer/local-profile.md#one-cluster-port-and-kubeconfig-per-checkout).

### Q-HA-492 · The fill of the versions' sort keys records its completion after a pass that leaves no row without a key

Status: **Decided by the development agent on 2026-11-24** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: migration 00116 adds the sort key of a version and its pre-release flag ([api-and-ui.md](api-and-ui.md) Q-API-429), which only
the format's code can compute, so the rows stored before it have neither, and a replica of the release before it writes more such rows
while a rolling upgrade runs (R-HA-020). R-HA-022 starts a background migration only once no replica of an older release is live, which
the NuGet recomputation reads from a release number written into the code (`Semver2LastOldRelease`). The release that will carry this
change is not known when it is written: semantic-release sets it at the release, and a patch release of the commits before it may come
first. The reads stay right without the keys ([api-and-ui.md](api-and-ui.md) Q-API-430); the fill makes them cheap again.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The fill starts at once and records its completion only after a pass that leaves no row without a key (chosen) | `data_migration_version_sort_key`: keyset batches by id over the rows whose key is NULL (index `package_versions_unkeyed`), locked with `SKIP LOCKED`, the key from `formathost.VersionOrder`; at the end of a pass a row without a key left (written behind the cursor, or held by a writer) queues the next run a minute later and records nothing; a worker that starts queues it while the completion is missing or such a row exists, and deletes a completion that such a row followed | The data say when the old writers are gone, so no release number can be wrong; a rollback and an upgrade again, or a restore of an older backup, are filled again by the next worker; filling early costs nothing, because a filled row is never written again | A run during the roll may find rows left and wait a minute; the report shows `pending` while it waits |
| (b) Wait while a replica of the release before is live, as the NuGet recomputation does | `postgres.ReplicasUpTo(<the release before>)` | The rule of R-HA-022 as written | The release before is a number the change cannot know: it was 0.122.2 when this was written and 0.122.3 an hour later, when the fix before it on `main` was released; a wrong number lets an old replica write behind the fill, or makes the fill wait for no one |
| (c) Wait while any live replica runs a release lower than the fill's own binary | No constant | No number to keep | A dev build counts as newest; every later upgrade waits for the replicas before it whenever the fill runs again |
| (d) The migration Job fills the keys | Go code in `quader migrate` | Done before a replica starts | The Job must load every format's code; the replicas of the release before keep writing rows without a key after it |

**Choice:** (a). **Rationale:** what R-HA-022's version gate protects against is a row of the old shape left behind the backfill; where the
data show such a row, a check of the data at the end of a pass protects against it exactly, whoever wrote it and whenever, and needs no
release number. The development agent would revisit it if a migration's old shape cannot be seen in the data, which needs the version gate
of R-HA-022. **Applied in the spec:** R-HA-022 (the status, the start rule and its acceptance criterion). Code:
[sortkey.go](../../internal/packages/sortkey/sortkey.go) (`Fill`, `Background`), [version_sort_key.sql](../../internal/meta/postgres/queries/version_sort_key.sql),
`startSortKeyFill` in [wire_formats.go](../../internal/app/wire_formats.go), `app.BackgroundMigrations`. Tests:
`TestR_API_029_VersionsWithoutAStoredKeyKeepTheirPlaceBeforeAndAfterTheFill` ([packages](../../test/integration/packages/versions_unkeyed_test.go)),
`TestR_HA_020_TheSortKeyStepPassesOnADatabaseOfThePreviousRelease` ([postgres](../../test/integration/postgres/version_sort_key_test.go)),

### Q-HA-493 · The accounts of the upstream registries are one projected volume with optional sources in the pods of api, packages and worker

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: R-HA-073 mounts the Secrets of `secrets.upstreamAccounts`. Every Secret of the chart is mounted only into the pods that read it,
with items, `0440` and no `subPath` (R-HA-030); several accounts may be declared, each from a Secret of its own or from one Secret.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) One projected volume, one optional source per entry, in every pod of `api`, `packages` and `worker` (chosen) | `upstream-accounts` with `<key>/username` and `<key>/password` | One mount whatever the number of accounts; a missing Secret starts the pod; every role that fetches from an upstream reads it | A pod of `api` holds the token though it only tests and lists |
| (b) One Secret volume per entry | As `secrets.oidc[]` | The precedent | A missing Secret holds the pod in `ContainerCreating` unless each volume is optional; one volume per account |
| (c) Only the `worker` pods | Fewer holders | | A client's fill runs in `packages` and the upstream test in `api`; both would send no account |

**Choice:** (a). **Rationale:** the account is used wherever the repository's client is built, and that is each of the three roles; the
scanners, the updater and the Jobs never contact an upstream registry and get nothing.

**Applied in the spec:** R-HA-073, R-HA-030's table. Code: [_upstream_accounts.tpl](../../deploy/helm/quader/templates/_upstream_accounts.tpl).

### Q-HA-494 · `secrets.upstreamAccounts` is a map by the registry's key, and `authMode` defaults to basic

what an operator reads.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) A map by the registry's key; `authMode` `basic` by default; `usernameKey` `username`, `passwordKey` `password` (chosen) | `secrets.upstreamAccounts.docker-hub.existingSecret` | One entry per registry by construction; a Helm `--set` and a Flux patch address it by key; `basic` is what the OCI registries and GitLab take | A list like `secrets.oidc[]` is not followed |
| (b) A list of `{key, existingSecret, …}` | As `secrets.oidc[]` | The precedent | A key twice needs a check; a values overlay replaces the whole list |
| (c) `bearer` by default | | npm's token | Docker Hub refuses a raw access token without its handshake (R-REPO-033: no handshake for `bearer`) |

**Choice:** (a). **Rationale:** the registry's key is the identity of the account, and `basic` is the mode of the case that made the owner

### Q-HA-495 · A stopping scanner tries its sign-off again for ten seconds; a replica that vanished without a word stays lost by the registry's rule

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

Context: on the owner's UI profile every restart left the scanner rows of before on the System page, ready for 30 s and then **Lost**,
and kept them (2026-11-25: `freshclam` 2, `trivy` 4, `clamav` 3 rows after a few restarts). Read in the code: a row ends at the
scanner's sign-off (`DELETE`, R-OPS-048), is left out of the list once it went stale while `draining` and deleted by
`replica-registry-prune` at its next run (Q-OPS-210), and a row that went stale in any other state is listed as lost and deleted 24 h after
its last report. The profile stopped quader first and its scanners after it, so every draining report and every sign-off met a closed scan
listener, and it removed the malware scanner's container without a stop, so that one sent nothing: each restart made rows that ended in
order look like replicas that vanished. In the product the same happens to a scanner pod whose sign-off finds no `packages` replica to
take it: an upgrade rolls `packages` and the scanners at once, and the sign-off was one request, on a connection that may be the one to a
`packages` pod closing its listener. What the owner asked: the replicas that exist; one that went away in order gone at once, one that
vanished without a word lost for a bounded time and then removed, and the counts count the living.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The sign-off is tried again while the scan listener cannot take it (no connection, `5xx`, `429`, `408`), the pause doubling from 250 ms to 2 s, for at most 10 s and within the close phase; a lost row keeps the registry's 24 h (chosen) | `scanreport.Reporter.Stop` | A stop in order reaches a `packages` replica that is up, whichever one the Service picks next; the registry's rule stays one rule for both tables; a pod that never reaches one ends 10 s later than before, inside its grace period | A scanner that ends in order while no `packages` replica is reachable for those 10 s is listed as lost for 24 h (H-1995) |
| (b) A new row of a kind and a name replaces the older rows of both | A container restarted in its pod takes its predecessor's place | No second row of one pod | A crash inside a pod (an out-of-memory kill) shows as nothing at all, against the owner's "lost for a bounded time"; two reporting processes of one name would take each other's row in turn |
| (c) A shorter bound for a lost row (an hour) | The prune and the list | A vanished replica leaves sooner | The administrator who looks the next morning no longer sees that a replica vanished in the night; the registry of R-OPS-003 keeps its 24 h, so the System page would hold two rules |
| (d) The list hides a lost row of a kind whose live rows meet its configured count | | No lost row while the kind is whole | The list would need the Deployment's replica count, which no replica knows |

**Choice:** (a), and the profile stops its scanners before quader and the malware scanner's container with `TERM`, as the kubelet does
(`deploy/ui-dev/serve.sh`, `malware.sh`). **Rationale:** the cause in both places was a sign-off that did not arrive, not the rule of the
list; the rule is the registry's, which the owner's walk of W-13 settled (Q-OPS-210). What an installation shows now during a rolling update
of `malware-scanner-clamav` with two replicas (`maxSurge: 1`, `maxUnavailable: 0`, `minReadySeconds: 10`): minute 0, the new pod's row
appears **Starting** (`database`) beside the two ready ones, three rows, "2 of 3 ready"; when it is ready, about 30 to 50 s later with its
signature database, and 10 s after that, the first old pod gets `SIGTERM`, reports `draining` and signs off, and its row is gone at once:
two rows; the second pair follows the same way, about a minute later. The rows never number four, and none is **Lost**. A pod killed
without its sign-off (the node lost, a kill past the grace period) shows ready until its report is 30 s old
(`system.heartbeat_stale_after`), then **Lost**, counted in no number, until the prune deletes it 24 h after its last report.

**Applied in the spec:** [operations-and-observability.md](operations-and-observability.md) R-OPS-048 ("Gone the way a replica goes"), H-1995
there. Code: [reporter.go](../../internal/scanreport/reporter.go) `Stop`, `signOff`; test `TestR_OPS_048_TheSignOffIsTriedAgainWithinItsBound`
in [scanreport_test.go](../../internal/scanreport/scanreport_test.go); the profile's [serve.sh](../../deploy/ui-dev/serve.sh)
`stop_scanners` and [malware.sh](../../deploy/ui-dev/malware.sh) `down`.

Status: **Decided by the development agent** — selected from the options below; the owner reviews it at the walkthrough.

(`startScannerReport`, Q-OPS-225), so a pod has one row.

| Option | What it means | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) The profile sets `QUADER_POD_NAME=<project>-vuln-scanner-trivy` for both processes, as the chart does (chosen) | `deploy/ui-dev/serve.sh` | The System page names the unit as the malware scanner's and the updater's rows already do; nothing of the product changes | — |
| (b) A name for each process (`…-scanner`, `…-loader`) | | Two names in the logs | The chart's two containers share the pod's name; the profile would show what no installation shows |

### H-37 · A database restore revives revoked credentials and removed grants

Restoring PostgreSQL to time *t*, from the platform layer (R-HA-025) or from a Quader backup taken at
*t* (R-HA-060), restores every token, session, user and permission policy as it was at *t*. Token
revocations, user and service-account disables, group-membership and role-binding removals, policy
narrowings and CI mapping changes made after *t* are undone. A token revoked because it leaked
becomes valid again. With scheduled backups, *t* can lie up to one backup interval in the past.
Both restore paths end all UI sessions and print a warning, but the database alone cannot know
what happened after *t*: those facts were only in the lost part of the database, in the audit log
stream and in the revocation journal.

- **Mitigated in the MVP** by the revocation journal (R-HA-054, Q-HA-9): both restore paths
  re-apply the journal kept in object storage. What stays live: removals whose outbox rows had not
  been shipped when the old database stopped (normally less than one shipping interval, default
  5 s), every removal made while `backup.revocation_journal.enabled` was false, the whole journal
  when the blob bucket that holds it is lost together with the database, and, without bucket
  versioning, journal objects deleted with the runtime S3 credential. Access granted after *t* is
  lost rather than revived, and objects whose history replay cannot reproduce exactly are
  suspended; both fail closed.
- The manual fallback for what stays live: read the `log: audit` stream from *t* to the restore,
  and repeat each revocation and removal through `quader admin token revoke` and the API.

### H-38 · Plain HTTP between the edge proxy and the replicas

This gap applies only to an installation that sets `tls.enabled: false` (R-HA-063). With the default
`tls.enabled: true`, the edge connects to the pods over TLS and Quader serves it (R-ARCH-035), so there is no
plain-HTTP path between the edge and the replicas. With `tls.enabled: false`, requests travel to the pods
unencrypted, including `Authorization` headers with bearer tokens, Basic credentials and session cookies.
Anyone who can capture pod-network traffic can read them: a compromised node, a privileged pod with host
networking, or a CNI-level tap. The mitigation for such an installation is at the platform level: a service
mesh with mutual TLS, or CNI encryption (WireGuard or IPsec modes of common CNIs). The chart does not enforce
either.

### H-79 · Artifacts are unsigned and nothing checks their origin

The release pipeline ([build.yml](../../.github/workflows/build.yml)) publishes the image
`docker.io/guidedtraffic/quader` and the chart at `https://guided-traffic.github.io/quader/`, and no
consumer receives a signature to check them against. The image carries a provenance and an SBOM
attestation in its image index. The chart carries none: `helm package` runs without `--sign`, so there is
no `.prov` file, and the pipeline makes no chart SBOM. The attestations are unsigned, so they name the build
but not the party that made the claim.

- **Component and subject:** the release pipeline and the two places it writes to. The subject is every
  consumer that pulls the image or the chart, and any admission policy of the cluster that runs them. The
  chart renders no admission policy and no signature check.
- **Live or dormant:** live: Release Docker & Helm publishes every release (run 42436292019 published `v0.25.2`,
  [releasing.md](../developer/releasing.md#the-release-pipeline)).
- **What makes it real:** whoever holds the Docker Hub access token of the account `guidedtraffic` (the
  secret `DOCKERHUB_PAT`) can push a different image under an existing tag. The chart pulls by tag by default,
  because `image.digest` is empty in [values.yaml](../../deploy/helm/quader/values.yaml). Whoever can write to the
  `gh-pages` branch can change a published chart, and the release job writes that branch with
  `git push --force`. Docker Scout reports CVEs without checking origin. The keyless signatures of the earlier
  pipeline are not part of the design since 2026-10-29 ([Q-HA-11](#q-ha-11--publishing-location-of-images-and-chart)).
  OPS-076 ("Signed release artifacts", P1) is therefore open: no signature is delivered, and R-HA-047 no longer
  covers it.

### H-80 · Self-hosted runners build the code of every pull request

[release.yml](../../.github/workflows/release.yml) runs every job on the organisation's self-hosted runners, on every push and
every pull request to `main` (`runs-on: self-hosted` and `runs-on: large`), except the kind legs that load the NuGet clients
image, which run on GitHub-hosted runners (owner, 2026-11-05, [releasing.md](../developer/releasing.md#ci)). The MinIO leg of R-STOR-035 builds MinIO from source on those runners (job `s3-conformance`). R-HA-051
and Q-HA-3 had described that build on isolated runners, so the isolation those pages describe is not in the
design.

- **Component and subject:** the self-hosted runners and the pipeline. The subject is the organisation's secrets
  that the jobs of a pull request receive, and the host and network of a runner while a job runs.
- **Live or dormant:** live for every pull request from a branch of this repository. Those runs receive the
  repository's secrets: the jobs `image`, `container-scan`, `integration`, `s3-conformance`, `e2e` and `e2e-npm` on the
  self-hosted runners, and `e2e-nuget`, `e2e-ci`, `e2e-bastion` and `e2e-vuln` on GitHub-hosted runners, log in to
  Docker Hub with `secrets.DOCKERHUB_PAT`. GitHub passes repository secrets to pull requests from the same
  repository, not to pull requests from forks. Whether a fork's pull request reaches these runners at all depends
  on the repository's Actions settings, which are not in the repository and are not verified here. For the jobs on
  GitHub-hosted runners the host-and-network part is dormant (a fresh virtual machine per job that GitHub discards
  afterwards); their secret part stays live.
  The job `sbom-generator` pulls public images anonymously and holds no secret.
- **What makes it real:** a pull request can change the workflow file or the Makefile of its own branch, and the
  changed file runs with the secrets. Whoever can push a branch to this repository can therefore read
  `DOCKERHUB_PAT` from a job. The runners are ephemeral pods ([releasing.md](../developer/releasing.md#ci)), which
  bounds what a build leaves behind. What a running job can reach from the pod's network is not verified here.

### H-564 · The platform check reads settings, not outcomes

Component: the task `backup-check` and `quader admin backup check` (R-HA-023). Subject: whether a point-in-time restore would work. The check reads `archive_mode`, the bucket's versioning and lifecycle rules and the grace period. `archive_mode = on` says PostgreSQL hands finished WAL segments to its archive command; it does not say that the command succeeds, that a base backup exists or that a restore has ever been tried. A noncurrent-version rule that matches only a prefix of the bucket counts as one that matches the bucket.

Live whenever `backup.recovery_window` is declared. What makes it real: an archive command that fails (an expired credential, a deleted bucket) while `archive_mode` stays `on`, so `quader_backup_check_ok{check="archive_mode"}` stays 1 and `QuaderBackupCheckFailed` stays silent. The restore drill of R-HA-025 is the only check of the outcome, and it is not run by the installation.

### H-693 · A connection held at the close deadline is named by pool, not by holder

Component: the close of the database pools (`DB.CloseContext`, Q-HA-203). Subject: which code still holds a connection when the
close phase ends. pgx exposes the number of acquired connections of a pool, not their holders, so the error says `main pool (1
connection held)` and the holder has to be found in the goroutine dump.

The readiness check loop is a holder as well: it runs until after the close phase (the check loop stops last), and its `database`
and `schema` checks hold the control connection for up to `health.check_timeout` each. That loop is not stopped by this decision.

Live whenever a detached write (the periodic token last-used flush, 10 s; the rollback of `InTx`, 5 s; the detached writes of
the upload paths, up to 30 s, not traced) is running at the close deadline. What makes it real: such a write is cut by the process
exit, and its effect is lost; the next use records most of them again, a half-finished upload is cleaned up by its sweep.

### H-791 · The Sentinel alert is tested as a rule, not as an alert of a running installation

Component: `QuaderValkeySentinelsDegraded` ([_rules.tpl](../../deploy/helm/quader/templates/_rules.tpl), R-OPS-046). Subject: whether the alert fires in an installation when the Sentinel quorum is lost. `promtool test rules` feeds the gauge's series to the expression; the set `ha-faults` checks the gauge `quader_valkey_sentinels_reachable` on the pods. The profile `alerts` runs a Prometheus through the ServiceMonitor and proves `QuaderValkeyUnavailable` and the other alerts its tests wait for firing; for this one it only reads that it resolves after the outage (`TestAlerts_R_OPS_046_ValkeyOutage`).

Live today, for this alert. What makes it real: a metric the pods do not export under the name the rule reads would leave it silent while both tiers stay green.

### H-792 · A backup or restore pod cut off from the network is not injected

Component: the Jobs `quader-backup` and the restore Job (R-HA-007 rows "Backup pod evicted, crashed or cut off", "Restore pod evicted, crashed or cut off"). Subject: the "cut off" part of the rows. `TestBackupDrain` evicts the pod by a node drain and crashes it with `kill -9` (R-BAK-010, R-BAK-012, R-BAK-021); no scenario denies the pod PostgreSQL or the object store with a NetworkPolicy while the run is under way. The copy loops end on a failed call and the Job controller starts a new pod, which the crash scenarios show, but a hung connection that never fails (a black-holed route) is a different path (the client timeouts of R-STOR-033, the lease of the run).

Live today for the backup and the restore Job. Not verified, and this is the gap: what a run does when its connection stalls without an error (a black-holed route), as opposed to one that is refused or reset; the client timeouts of R-STOR-033 and the run's lease bound it on paper.

### H-793 · The dev store was not shown to reject a wrong secret key

Component: the e2e run of R-HA-007's row "S3 credentials fail" (the first version of `TestHAFaults_ObjectStoreCredentialRejected`, removed). Subject: whether the SeaweedFS of the dev profile answers a request signed with a wrong secret key with a rejection. The test replaced `secret-access-key` in the Secret `quader-s3` (the one Quader mounts, `secrets.s3.existingSecret`) under the load, with the operator's annotations taken off; in the nightly dispatches 42587147342 and 42595613488 no request failed for five minutes and no replica logged an object-store error. Whether the Secret did not reach the pods, or the store does not check the signature, is not established.

Live today for that row: the circuit, the log line and the credential codes are proven by unit tests ([guard_test.go](../../internal/blob/guard_test.go), [client_test.go](../../internal/blob/s3/client_test.go)) against a fake store; no run shows a real store's answer to a revoked key or a wrong secret.

### H-795 · The e2e legs of E5.10 are not yet shown green on a runner

The scenarios were run in three nightly dispatches on the large class while other legs of the same and other runs shared its nodes (the probes of unrelated pods timed out in the second one: the sentinels, the object store and Keycloak). In all of them k6 recorded 50 to 200 requests that the edge answered `502` after 11 to 15 s, in every test, at times unrelated to the injected fault (the planned failover's came 40 s after it), and the first dispatch's `ha-suite` and `npm-ha` legs were skipped, so no unloaded reference run exists. `TestHAFaults_ValkeySentinelQuorumLoss`, `ValkeyFlushAll` and `ValkeyCredentialMismatch` and the graceful and control-pooler legs of `TestHAPooler_InstanceLoss` passed in a dispatch where the cluster was not starved (42587147342); all four legs of `TestHAPooler_InstanceLoss` passed in 42601429868; the planned failover's 10 s bound held (7.4 to 8.0 s for every replica, 42601429868). Not verified: a green run of every test of `ha-faults` and `ha-pooler` in one dispatch, and whether the `502` bursts come from the contention or from Quader or the edge.

### H-803 · The sizing profiles are not measured

Component: the sizing profiles of R-HA-050 ([profiles/](../../deploy/helm/quader/profiles)). Subject: an operator who picks a profile for the load it names. The acceptance asks for a reference load test (npm and NuGet clients replaying a recorded mix of installs, restores and publishes) against each profile in CI before the beta, and for the table to be updated from its results. That test does not exist: it needs the reference environment of [Q-ROAD-9](../coverage/roadmap.md#q-road-9--what-wp28-builds-of-r-arch-027s-load-scripts-and-where-they-run) (the same one as [H-491](../security/vulnerability-scanning.md#h-491--the-performance-run-is-not-the-reference-environment)), which is not built, and the recorded mix of client traffic. The profile files and their tests prove that the numbers render and agree with the table, not that a profile serves the clients it names. Live today: every installation that takes a profile on trust. What makes it real: a `packages` pod that the table sizes for 50 concurrent clients saturates at fewer, or a database `max_connections` that the formula of R-HA-016 gets right and the load does not.

### H-804 · A change of the CA source reaches the pods at the kubelet's pace

Component: the trusted CA bundle of R-HA-043. Subject: the operator who rotates a CA in the Secret or ConfigMap named by `trustedCA`. R-REPO-035 promises that a CA file added to the mounted source is trusted within 60 s without a restart; the binary reads the file again at most every 10 s on use, but the mounted file changes when the kubelet syncs the volume, which takes up to the kubelet's sync period plus its cache delay (about a minute with the defaults, more on a loaded node). The chart tests render the mount and the paths; the reload from the file is the unit tests' of R-REPO-035; no end-to-end test changes a ConfigMap and times the first request that trusts the new CA. Live today: every rotation. What makes it real: an upstream whose CA was rotated fails with `tls_untrusted` for the kubelet's delay on every pod after the source changed.

### H-805 · The platform matrix installs the chart and starts no pod

Component: the platform matrix of R-HA-049 (job `k8s-matrix`, [k8s-matrix.sh](../../deploy/dev/k8s-matrix.sh)). Subject: the claim that the chart works on Kubernetes 1.34 and 1.37 with Helm 4 and Helm 3. The acceptance says the matrix "runs R-HA-052's smoke subset"; the legs install the chart with its pods unable to start (no database, Valkey, object store or image there), so they prove that each API server admits and stores the objects and that both Helm majors install, upgrade and remove the release, not that Quader runs on those versions. The failure suite runs on Kubernetes 1.37 with Helm 4 only. Live today: Kubernetes 1.34 with either Helm, and 1.37 with Helm 3, have no running pod in any test. What makes it real: a behaviour of the kubelet or the scheduler of 1.34 that the API server does not show (the spread of `nodeTaintsPolicy`, the eviction of an unhealthy pod).

### H-798 · A drained `api` or `packages` pod can run its whole grace period before it is killed

Component: the shutdown of `api` and `packages` replicas under a node drain (R-HA-011, R-HA-059). Subject: every drain, eviction and rollout where it happens.

Live in the observed settings, holder not found. (1) On the cluster with the transaction-mode poolers (`QUADER_POOLER=1`, R-HA-058), measured on 2026-11-09 on arm64 with `kubectl delete pod` of an `api` pod: 120 s (the grace period) with the container still logging its health checks, no `stopped` record and exit 137; 16 s on the same image without the poolers. (2) In the nightly run `e2e-alerts` of the branch `p7-e55b` (runs 42605224759, 42624338696, 42647438388; amd64, GitHub-hosted, profile `alerts` with a Prometheus scraping the pods every 10 s), the drains of variants A, B, C and E each took 2 minutes to 2 minutes 26 seconds and `api` and `packages` containers of the drained node ended with exit 137, while the `worker` pods of the same drain ended earlier.

Verified in this repo and in the artifacts. The poolers are not the common factor: the latest nightly run 42647438388 (variants A, E, C and B; its log names no pooler) shows drains of 2 minutes 3 seconds to 2 minutes 26 seconds without them, and the laptop run with them is the other observation, so what the two settings share is not known. The default profile without poolers reports no SIGKILL in its drain test (the leg `drain-roles` of the nightly 42595813923 logs "none with SIGKILL"; that leg fails on other conditions). The kubelet events of the killed pods in run 42605224759 show `Killing` at the eviction, readiness `503` for the length of the drain delay (15 s), then `connection refused` on the ops port until the kill at 120 s: the ops listener had closed and the process lived on. The log of the laptop run shows the health check of the object store still running 100 s after the pools had closed, so the process had passed the close phase of R-ARCH-024 step 6 and `healthStop` had not run: the step it stood in lies between the end of the close phase and the stop of the check loop, that is the shutdown of the ops listener. The unit test `R-ARCH-024 R-HA-011 a peer on the ops listener that never reads its responses ...` shows that one connection on the ops listener that does not finish held the whole process until the exit deadline (119.5 s of 120 s), which is that picture; since [Q-ARCH-456](architecture.md#q-arch-456--the-steps-after-the-close-phase-each-wait-at-most-the-ops-reserve-and-log-what-they-abandon-with-the-goroutines) the ops listener, the wait for the background goroutines and the tracer wait at most 0.5 s each after the close phase and log what they abandon with a dump of the goroutines.

Not verified, and this is the gap: which peer held the ops listener in the observed runs, and why the default profile's drain tests and the later local runs of the poolers do not show it. The same code with the poolers in use on the local kind cluster (five runs: a delete under load that reads the database, a node drain that evicts the pooler pods, a delete during a failover of the database primary, a delete with a scraper on HTTP/2, a delete on a freshly built image) stopped in 15 s each time, so the local cluster does not reproduce it by itself; the logs of the drained pods of the nightly were lost with the pods. Next step: the drain variants of the set `alerts` stream the logs of the evicted pods into the artifacts (`drain-variant-<variant>-<pod>.log`, [Q-HA-280](#q-ha-280--the-drain-variants-keep-the-logs-of-the-evicted-pods-in-the-artifacts)); the next nightly shows either the `stopped` record within the grace period, or the line `ops listener: connections still open at the ops deadline were reset` / `background goroutines still running at the end of the shutdown` / `components did not stop before the close deadline` with the goroutines that name the holder. This finding is removed when a nightly `alerts` run shows the drained `api` and `packages` pods ending before their grace period and without exit 137.

What makes it real: a node drain or rollout then cuts the transfers of the draining pod at the end of the grace period instead of letting them finish (R-HA-011). The scenario "Maintenance stays quiet" does not judge it: it requires that each drain ran and then reads the alerts.

### H-799 · The set `edge` has ended the self-hosted `large` runner four times; its full-size result exists on the laptop only

Component: the CI leg `e2e-edge` of the nightly workflow ([performance.yml](../../.github/workflows/performance.yml)) on the shared self-hosted `large` runner. Subject: the evidence of exit criterion E5.5 for R-HA-039 in CI.

Live. On 2026-11-09 four dispatches of the leg on the branch `p7-e55` (runs 42613296450, 42624333458, 42628360515, 42647432138) ended with "The self-hosted runner lost communication with the server" 6 to 15 minutes into `make e2e SET=edge`; steps that ran on the runner afterwards (`df`, `docker system df`) hung, so no log of the host exists. The first three streamed or wrote 6 GiB and 2 GiB of random bytes (the first two as files in the client pod, the third streamed); a neighbour run was on the machine in the first two (the main nightly, another builder's branch), and none was in the fourth except one queued. The same set, full size, passes on the arm64 laptop in 25 minutes (`TestEdge_R_HA_039_TransfersThroughTheIngressAndTheGateway` with 6144 MiB uploaded and downloaded through both edges in 1m16s and 46s, 17m7s for the reads at 2 MiB/s, the 1 GiB push in 14 s) with 22 to 25 GB of disk free in the Docker VM, and a sampler of the kind nodes saw at most 4.4 GiB of memory on the control-plane node. Not verified: which resource of the runner machine runs out (memory of the host, its disk, or the I/O of 12 GiB written beside the other legs) and what the runner agent's limits are.

What makes it real: the leg shows red as a lost runner and takes a neighbour's job with it if it shares the machine; until the cause is known the criterion's CI evidence for the transfers is the local full-size run, and the leg should run alone on the machine (a dispatch with no other leg in progress).

### H-1050 · Only the probe write and the take script are checked at start; another missing command shows at its first use

Component: the access check of a replica's first Valkey connection ([Q-HA-331](#q-ha-331--an-answer-is-the-login-or-its-refusal-and-the-first-connection-also-writes-the-probe-key-and-runs-the-take-script),
`checkAccess` in [valkey_answer.go](../../internal/cluster/valkey_answer.go)). Subject: an ACL user that lacks another command of
[architecture.md](architecture.md) R-ARCH-031's list (`GET`, `INCR`, `ZADD`, `PUBLISH`, `SUBSCRIBE`, `MULTI`, `DELIFEQ` and the
others). Live in every installation whose operator writes the ACL by hand. What makes it real: the replica becomes ready, and the
mechanism that needs the command meets `NOPERM` at its first use: the call counts as `quader_valkey_errors_total{kind="auth"}`,
the circuit opens after `valkey.circuit_breaker.failure_threshold` such calls, and that mechanism runs its fallback (R-HA-057), so
limits count per replica or a fetch collapses per replica until the ACL is fixed. Nothing is served wrongly.

### H-1051 · A mistyped Valkey or Sentinel address is silence, and the replica becomes ready degraded after the bound

Component: the first answer of R-HA-008 ([Q-HA-331](#q-ha-331--an-answer-is-the-login-or-its-refusal-and-the-first-connection-also-writes-the-probe-key-and-runs-the-take-script)).
Subject: a release whose `valkey.sentinel.addresses` or `valkey.address` names a host that does not resolve or a port nobody
listens on. Live with any such typo. What makes it real: a name that does not resolve and a refused connection are what a pod
being rescheduled looks like for seconds, so they count as silence; every new replica holds its first readiness for
`valkey.startup_answer_timeout` and then becomes ready with the `valkey` check `degraded` (`no_sentinel` or `connecting`), and a
rollout replaces every working replica with a degraded one, 30 s per pod, instead of stalling. `QuaderValkeyUnavailable` fires
once every replica has been degraded for 2 minutes, and the WARN line of each start names the bound and the reason.
